slots.text: Suppose there were no eternal consciousness in a human being; suppose that underneath everything there were nothing but a wild, fermenting power which, twisting in obscure passions, produced all things, the great and the trivial alike; suppose that a bottomless void, never sated, lay concealed beneath everything — then what would life be, if not despair? Suppose it were so: suppose no holy bond held humanity together; suppose one generation sprang up after another like leaves in a wood; suppose one generation replaced another like birdsong in a wood; suppose our kind went through the world the way a ship goes through the sea, the way wind goes through the desert — a thoughtless, barren business; suppose an everlasting forgetfulness lay in wait, forever hungry, for its prey, and no power were strong enough to tear the prey from it — how empty life would be then, and how bleak! But that is exactly why it is not so. As God created man and woman, in the same way he shaped the hero and the poet — or the orator. Of what the hero does, the poet can do nothing; all he can do is admire the hero, love him, take delight in him. And yet he too is happy — no less happy than the hero. For the hero is, as it were, his better being, with which he is in love — glad that it is not himself after all, glad that his love can be admiration. He is the presiding spirit of recollection. All he can do is call to mind what has been done; all he can do is admire what has been done. He takes nothing from what is his own; he is jealous, rather, of what was entrusted to him. He follows the choice of his heart; but when he has found what he was looking for, he goes round to every man’s door with his song and his speech, so that everyone may admire the hero as he does and take pride in the hero as he does. That is his feat, his humble task; that is his loyal service in the house of the hero. If in this way he keeps faith with his love, struggling night and day with the craft of forgetfulness, which wants to spirit the hero away from him, then his task is complete, and he is united with the hero, who has loved him with the same fidelity. For the poet is, as it were, the hero’s better being: without force, admittedly, as a memory is, but transfigured too, as a memory is. So no one who was great shall be forgotten. Even if it takes a long while, even if a cloud of misunderstanding should carry the hero off, his lover will come all the same; and the longer time went on, the more faithfully he clings to him.

No! Not one who was great in the world shall be forgotten. But each was great in his own way, each in proportion to the greatness of what he loved. For the one who loved himself grew great by himself, and the one who loved others grew great by his devotion; but the one who loved God grew greater than everyone. Everyone shall be remembered, but each grew great in proportion to his expectation. One grew great by expecting the possible, another by expecting the eternal; but the one who expected the impossible grew greater than everyone. Everyone shall be remembered, but each was great in proportion to the magnitude of what he struggled with. For the one who struggled with the world grew great by conquering the world, and the one who struggled with himself grew greater by conquering himself; but the one who struggled with God grew greater than everyone. So there was struggle in the world, man against man, one against a thousand; but the one who struggled with God was greater than everyone. So there was struggle on earth: there was the one who conquered everything by his power, and there was the one who conquered God by his powerlessness. There was the one who relied on himself and won everything; there was the one who, secure in his strength, sacrificed everything; but the one who believed God was greater than everyone. There was the one who was great by his power, and the one who was great by his wisdom, and the one who was great by his hope, and the one who was great by his love; but Abraham was greater than everyone — great by the power whose strength is powerlessness, great by the wisdom whose secret is foolishness, great by the hope whose form is madness, great by the love that is hatred of oneself.

It was by faith that Abraham left the land of his fathers and became an alien in the land of the promise. One thing he left behind and one thing he took along: behind him he left his earthly good sense, and faith he took along. Otherwise, presumably, he would not have set out, but would have thought: this is unreasonable, after all. It was by faith that he was an alien in the land of the promise. Nothing there reminded him of what he held dear; instead everything, being new, tempted his soul toward a melancholy longing. And yet he was the one God had chosen, the one in whom the Lord took pleasure! Indeed, if he had been cast off, shut out from God’s grace, he could more easily have comprehended it; as it was, it looked like a mockery of him and of his faith. There was also one in the world who lived banished from the land of his fathers, which he loved. He has not been forgotten, and neither have his laments, when in his melancholy he searched for and found what he had lost. There is no lament from Abraham. Lamenting is human, weeping with the one who weeps is human; but having faith is greater, and contemplating the believer more blessed.

It was by faith that Abraham received the promise that every family on earth would be blessed in his seed. Time went on; the possibility was there; Abraham had faith. Time went on; it became unreasonable; Abraham had faith. There was one in the world who also had an expectation. Time went on, evening came near, and he was not so wretched as to forget his expectation, and for that reason he too shall not be forgotten. Then he sorrowed, and sorrow did not deceive him, as life had done. Sorrow did all it could for him, and in sorrow’s sweetness his disappointed expectation was his to keep. Sorrowing is human, sorrowing with the one who sorrows is human; but having faith is greater, and contemplating the believer more blessed. Of Abraham we have no song of sorrow. He did not count off the days in melancholy as the times went by; he did not eye Sarah suspiciously to see whether she was getting old; he did not stop the sun in its course to keep Sarah from aging, and his expectation with her; he did not lull Sarah with his melancholy song. Abraham grew old, and Sarah was mocked throughout the land; and yet he was the one God had chosen, the heir to the promise that every family on earth would be blessed in his seed. So it would surely have been better if God had not chosen him? What does it mean, being chosen by God? Does it mean that the wish of youth is refused you in youth, so that with great difficulty it may be fulfilled in old age? But Abraham had faith and held fast to the promise. If Abraham had wavered, he would have given it up, saying to God: “Perhaps, then, it is not your will after all that it should come to pass; in that case I will give up the wish. It was the only one I had; it was my blessedness. My soul is honest; I hide no secret grudge against you for refusing it.” He would not have been forgotten; many would have been saved by his example; but he would not have become the father of faith. For to give up one’s wish is great, but to hold it fast after one has given it up is greater; to grasp the eternal is great, but to hold fast to the temporal after one has given it up is greater. — Then the fullness of time came. If Abraham had not had faith, Sarah would probably have died of sorrow, and Abraham, blunted by grief, would not have understood the fulfillment and would have smiled at it the way one smiles at a dream from one’s youth. But Abraham had faith, and that is why he was young. For the one who always hopes for the best is deceived by life and grows old; the one who is always ready for the worst grows old early; but the one who has faith keeps an eternal youth. So praise be to that story! For Sarah, old as she was, was young enough to long for a mother’s joy, and Abraham, gray as he was, was young enough to wish to become a father. Outwardly, the wonder is that it happened as they had expected. In a deeper sense, faith’s wonder is this: Abraham and Sarah were young enough to wish, and faith had preserved their wish, and so their youth. He received the fulfillment of the promise; he received it in faith, and it came about according to the promise and according to faith. For Moses struck the rock with his rod, but he did not have faith.
Then there was gladness in Abraham’s house, when Sarah stood a bride on their golden wedding day.

But that was not how it was to stay; Abraham was to be put to the proof once more. He had fought against that crafty power which invents everything, against that watchful enemy who never slumbers, against that old man who outlives all things — he had fought against time and preserved his faith. Now the whole terror of the struggle was gathered into a single instant. “And God tempted Abraham and said to him: Take Isaac, your only son, whom you love; go to the land of Moriah, and there sacrifice him as a burnt offering on a mountain I will show you.”

So everything was wasted — more terrible than if it had never happened! So the Lord was merely making a mockery of Abraham! By a wonder he had made the unreasonable actual; now he wished to see it reduced to nothing again. It was foolishness, of course; but Abraham did not laugh at it, as Sarah laughed when the promise was announced. All was wasted! Seventy years of faithful expectation, the short-lived joy at faith’s fulfillment. Who is this, then, who tears the staff from the old man’s hand? Who is this who demands that the old man break it himself! Who is this who makes a man’s gray hairs inconsolable? Who is this who demands that he do it himself! Is there no pity for the venerable old man, none for the innocent child! And yet Abraham was the one God had chosen, and it was the Lord who laid the test on him. Now everything was to be wasted! The glorious remembrance of the generations, the promise in Abraham’s seed — only a whim, a passing thought the Lord had had, which Abraham must now blot out. That glorious treasure — as old as the faith in Abraham’s heart, older than Isaac by many, many years, the fruit of Abraham’s life, hallowed by prayers, ripened in battles — the blessing on Abraham’s lips: this was the fruit that must now be torn off untimely and made meaningless; for what meaning could it have, if Isaac was to be sacrificed! That melancholy yet blessed hour when Abraham was to say farewell to all that was dear to him, when he would once more lift his venerable head, when his countenance would shine like the Lord’s, when he would gather up his whole soul in a blessing strong enough to make Isaac blessed for all his days — that hour was never to come! For Abraham would indeed say farewell to Isaac, but it would be Abraham who remained behind; death would indeed part them, but it would be Isaac that death took as its prey. The old man would not, glad in death, lay his hand on Isaac in blessing; weary of life, he would lay a violent hand on Isaac. And it was God who was testing him. Yes, woe — woe to the messenger who had come to Abraham with news like this! Who would have dared to be the bearer of this sorrow? But it was God who was testing Abraham.

But Abraham had faith, and faith for this life. Indeed, had his faith concerned only a life to come, he would presumably have found it easier to throw everything away and hurry out of a world he did not belong to. But Abraham’s faith was not of that sort — if there is such a sort. For strictly speaking it is not faith, only faith’s remotest possibility, which dimly senses its object at the very edge of the horizon, yet is separated from it by a gaping chasm in which despair plays its game. But Abraham had faith precisely for this life: faith that he would live to old age in the land, held in honor among the people, blessed in his descendants, unforgettable in Isaac, the one dearest to him in life. He embraced Isaac with a love for which it was only a poor expression to say that he faithfully fulfilled a father’s duty to love his son — as indeed the summons itself also has it: “the son whom you love.” Jacob had twelve sons, and one he loved; Abraham had only one, whom he loved.

But Abraham had faith and did not doubt; he believed the unreasonable. Had Abraham doubted — then he would have done something different, something great and splendid; for how could Abraham have done anything that was not great and splendid! He would have made his way to Mount Moriah, chopped the firewood, set the pyre alight, drawn the knife; he would have called out to God: “Do not despise this sacrifice. It is not the best I own — that much I know; for what is an old man next to the child of the promise? But it is the best I am able to give you. Let Isaac never learn of it, so that he may find comfort in his youth.” He would have driven the knife into his own chest. The world would have admired him, and his name would never have been forgotten; yet being admired is one thing, and becoming a guiding star that saves the anxious is another.
But Abraham had faith. He did not pray for himself, hoping to move the Lord; only when the just punishment went forth over Sodom and Gomorrah did Abraham step forward with his prayers.

We read in those holy scriptures: “And God tempted Abraham and said: Abraham, Abraham, where are you? But Abraham replied: Here I am.” You to whom my words are addressed — was it like that with you? When you saw the heavy visitations coming toward you from afar, did you not tell the mountains, “Hide me,” and the hills, “Fall on me”? Or were you stronger? Even so, did your foot not drag slowly along the road — did it not seem to yearn back toward the old tracks? When the call came to you, did you answer, or did you not — perhaps quietly, in a whisper? Not so Abraham. Glad, bold, full of trust, he answered in a loud voice: Here I am. We read on: “And Abraham rose early in the morning.” He hastened as though to a feast, and early in the morning he was at the place appointed, on Mount Moriah. He said nothing to Sarah, nothing to Eliezer — and who, after all, could have understood him? Had the temptation not, by its very nature, exacted from him a vow of silence? “He chopped the firewood, he bound Isaac, he set the pyre alight, he drew the knife.” My listener! There were many fathers who believed that in their child they were losing the dearest thing they had in the world, and being robbed of all hope for the future; yet there was, after all, no one who was the child of the promise in the sense that Isaac was for Abraham. There were many fathers who lost their child; but then it was God — the Almighty’s unchanging and unsearchable will — whose hand took it. Not so with Abraham. A heavier test had been kept for him: along with the knife, Isaac’s fate had been laid in Abraham’s hand. There he stood, that old man, with his only hope! Yet he did not doubt; he cast no anxious glances right or left; he did not challenge heaven by his prayers. He knew it was God Almighty who was testing him; he knew that this was the heaviest sacrifice that could be demanded of him; but he knew too that no sacrifice was too heavy when God demanded it — and he drew the knife.

Who strengthened Abraham’s arm, who held his right hand raised so that it did not sink down powerless! Whoever looks at this is paralyzed. Who strengthened Abraham’s soul, so that his eyes did not go dark and he saw neither Isaac nor the ram! Whoever looks at this goes blind. — And yet rare enough, perhaps, is the one who is paralyzed and blinded; rarer still is the one who tells worthily what happened. We all know it — it was only a test.

If Abraham, standing on Mount Moriah, had doubted; if he had looked around him helplessly; if, before drawing the knife, he had happened to spot the ram; if God had allowed him to sacrifice it in Isaac’s place — then he would have traveled home, and everything would have been as it was: he would have Sarah, he would keep Isaac — and yet how altered it all would be! For his retreat would have been a flight, his rescue an accident, his reward disgrace, and his future, perhaps, perdition. Then he would have borne witness not to his faith, nor to God’s grace, but to how terrible a thing it is to go up Mount Moriah. Then Abraham would not have been forgotten, and nor would Mount Moriah. It would then be named not as Ararat is named, where the Ark came to rest, but named as a horror, because it was here that Abraham doubted.

Venerable Father Abraham! When you traveled home from Mount Moriah, you had no need of a eulogy to console you for what you had lost; for you had won everything and kept Isaac — was that not how it was? The Lord took him from you no more; you sat at table with him, joyful, in your tent, as you do in the beyond through all eternity. Venerable Father Abraham! Since those days thousands of years have run on, but you need no late-born lover to wrench your memory from the clutches of forgetfulness; for every language remembers you — and yet you reward your lover more gloriously than anyone does: in the beyond you make him blessed in your bosom, and here you captivate his eye and his heart with the marvel of your deed. Venerable Father Abraham! Second father of our kind! You, the first to perceive and bear witness to that immense passion which disdains the terrible battle with raging elements and the powers of creation, in order to struggle with God; you, the first to know that supreme passion, the holy, pure, humble expression of that divine madness which the pagans admired — forgive the one who set out to speak your praise, if he did not do it as he should. He spoke humbly, as his heart longed to; he spoke briefly, as is proper. But he will never forget that you needed a hundred years to receive a son in your old age against every expectation, and that you had to draw the knife before Isaac was yours to keep; he will never forget that for a hundred and thirty years you got no further than faith.
